name: Obestatin

lead: Obestatin is a peptide made from the same gene as the hunger hormone ghrelin. A 2005 paper in Science reported that it reduced appetite in rodents, which led fat-loss readers to see it as a possible diet aid for lower intake and fat loss.
Other labs could not confirm the appetite effect, and its proposed receptor GPR39 was later found to respond to zinc instead. No studies test it for weight or appearance in people.

paras: There is no product; it is discussed as a hormone of the appetite system rather than something people use.
No approved product exists and the sources reviewed give no human safety data for administering it.

angle.text: Obestatin is a ghrelin-gene peptide first reported to curb appetite, so fat-loss readers see it as a possible diet aid for lower intake and fat loss. Later studies could not reproduce the appetite effect, and its receptor is disputed.

lead: Obestatin is a small peptide of about two dozen amino acids encoded by the same gene, GHRL, as the hunger hormone ghrelin.[1] It was reported in Science in 2005 after a computer search of genome sequences predicted a second peptide within the ghrelin precursor; the authors isolated it from rat stomach and named it from the Latin for 'devour' plus 'statin', meaning suppression.[2][1]

Its relevance to looks runs through body composition. Its original appetite-suppressing effect in rodents made it a candidate for weight-control research, and more recent work has turned to skeletal muscle, where studies in cells and animals report roles in muscle regeneration, fiber-type determination and strength in atrophy models.[3][4][5] That is the chain that connects it to physique, though no human treatment has been tested.

The appetite effect and the identity of its receptor have both been disputed: GPR39, first proposed, was reported to respond to zinc ions rather than obestatin, and some laboratories could not reproduce the food-intake findings.[6][7][8][9] Obestatin is an endogenous peptide with no approved use.

paras: According to Wikipedia, obestatin was reported in November 2005 in Science by a group led by Aaron Hsueh, with Zhang JV listed as first author, after a bioinformatic search of sequenced genomes predicted a second peptide in the ghrelin precursor.[1] The name combines 'obese', from the Latin obedere meaning to devour, with 'statin', denoting suppression, reflecting the original finding that treating rats with the peptide suppressed food intake and body-weight gain, in contrast to ghrelin's appetite-stimulating effect.[2]

The 2005 Science paper reported that a peptide derived from preproghrelin suppressed food intake and body-weight gain in rats, in contrast to ghrelin's appetite-stimulating effect, and proposed GPR39 as its receptor.[2][1] The peptide was found by bioinformatic prediction first and then isolated from rat stomach.[2]

Obestatin is produced in specialized epithelial cells of the stomach and small intestine in several species, including humans.[1] The GHRL gene yields a 117-amino-acid preproghrelin that is processed to proghrelin, then to ghrelin and a C-terminal fragment from which obestatin is presumed to be cleaved.[1][10]
An NMR structure solved in micelle solution shows a 24-residue peptide with about 29 percent helical content, in two short helices.[1]

The original report presented obestatin as an anorexigenic counterpart to ghrelin, and it was also said to oppose ghrelin on growth hormone secretion.[2][1] A 2007 rodent study examined its effect on energy balance and growth hormone secretion.[8] Reviews of ghrelin gene products discuss how the peptides differ in their effects on intake and gut motility.[11] A study of blood-brain barrier transport compared obestatin with ghrelin and adiponectin.[12]

A recent review describes obestatin being proposed as a therapeutic candidate for muscle disorders: studies report roles in myogenesis, increased regeneration after acute damage, better vascularization, less fibrosis, and greater strength in muscle atrophy linked to glucocorticoid treatment and Duchenne muscular dystrophy.[3] A 2017 study reported that obestatin controls muscle fiber-type determination, and a 2025 study linked obestatin treatment to mitochondrial homeostasis and muscle repair in a Duchenne model.[4][5] These are laboratory and animal findings.

Obestatin was reported to promote survival of pancreatic beta cells and human islets, and a 2014 review summarizes its cardiovascular actions, noting they are not simply the opposite of ghrelin's.[13][14]

sections.h: Why it draws interest for physique
paras: The interest in obestatin for appearance is a two-step chain. First, ghrelin is a well-known hunger hormone, and a peptide encoded by the same gene that was reported to restrain appetite looked like a possible lever on leanness.[2][11] Second, the later skeletal-muscle literature adds a different angle: a 2026 review describes obestatin as a candidate therapeutic for muscle pathology, with reported roles in myogenesis, regeneration after acute damage, vascularisation, reduced fibrosis and greater strength in glucocorticoid-linked atrophy and Duchenne muscular dystrophy models.[3] If a signal that supports muscle repair and fibre-type shifts were ever shown to work in people, the payoff would be maintaining or building muscle and a leaner body composition; at present that is a research hypothesis.

The same 2026 review notes that the field has gone through years of controversy over the food-intake function and the receptor, and that muscle is now the main focus.[3] A 2017 study in mice reported that obestatin controls fibre-type determination in skeletal muscle, and a 2025 study linked obestatin treatment to mitochondrial homeostasis and muscle repair in a Duchenne model.[4][5] These are laboratory findings in cells and animals.

Holst and colleagues reported that GPR39 signaling is stimulated by zinc but not by obestatin, and a second group found that obestatin did not activate GPR39.[6][7] A published comment on the 2005 paper also challenged the findings.[9] Wikipedia notes that deleting the ghrelin gene in mice did not significantly reduce food intake, that no known convertase has been shown to cleave proghrelin at the site that would generate obestatin, and that a review proposed renaming it 'ghrelin-associated peptide'.[1] The 2026 review describes years of controversy over the food-intake role and the receptor, with the muscle work emerging as the current focus.[3]

Circulating obestatin and the obestatin-to-ghrelin ratio have been measured in obesity, irritable bowel syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome and type 2 diabetes, and a 2011 meta-analysis examined ghrelin and obestatin levels in obesity.[1] One study reported that a circuit resistance exercise session changed growth hormone but not plasma obestatin.[1]

Wikipedia also records studies of the obestatin-to-ghrelin ratio in irritable bowel syndrome, obesity, Prader-Willi syndrome and type 2 diabetes, and measurements in people with and without delayed gastric emptying.[1] A 154-child observational study registered in 2013 measured ghrelin and obestatin in chronic kidney disease.[15] Blood-brain barrier research reported in 2006 compared how obestatin, ghrelin and adiponectin cross into the brain.[12]

No studies found of obestatin as a treatment for appearance, body weight or muscle in people. Registered human studies with ghrelin, not obestatin, examine appetite in cancer, frailty and other settings, and one observational study measured ghrelin and obestatin in children with chronic kidney disease.[16][15] Muscle, pancreas and heart work with obestatin itself is limited to cells and animals.[3][13][14]
Obestatin is an endogenous peptide, not an approved or marketed product. It is discussed in peptide and physique contexts mainly as a hormone connected to ghrelin and hunger.

Obestatin is not an approved or marketed product, and the encyclopedia entry does not describe any supplement use.[1] Mentions in physique and peptide settings are mostly of ghrelin-related hormones as part of explanations of hunger and appetite; discussion of obestatin itself is largely confined to the scientific literature, where Wikipedia notes one study found that a single circuit-resistance exercise session changed growth hormone but not plasma obestatin in female college students.[1]
